newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO spurns Israel proposal to salvage peace talks.
newsitem.headline: PLO spurns Israel proposal to salvage peace talks.

text.p: The PLO has rejected an Israeli proposal to salvage peace talks in crisis over a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, officials said.

An Israeli source said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had proposed the two sides bypass three planned Israeli troop withdrawals from the West Bank in order to complete "final status" peace talks within three to six months, nearly two years earlier than planned.
PLO officials confirmed Netanyahu made the proposal but denounced it as an attempt to scrap an existing interim peace deal and to deflect world criticism over his settlement policy.

"It's a new trick from Netanyahu and an attempt to divert people's attention from the destruction of the peace process that is taking place by Israeli bulldozers on Jabal Abu Ghneim," chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters.
Israeli tractors this week ripped into Jabal Abu Ghneim, a pine-covered hill occupied in 1967, prompting international condemnation and fears of violence. The hill is known as Har Homa in Hebrew.

"Netanyahu informed (Jordanian) King Hussein that he wants to jump over the interim period and move directly into permanent status talks. The PLO was informed by King Hussein," a PLO official told Reuters.

The Israeli source said Netanyahu made the offer because the Oslo interim peace accords, which commit Israel to the three pullbacks in parallel with talks on the fate of the occupied West Bank and Gaza, "created confrontations".
Erekat insisted Israel stick to an original timetable to pull its troops out of West Bank rural areas by mid-1998 in tandem with the final status talks.
"There is no contradiction between going with permanent status negotiations and continuing with implementation of the outstanding commitments of the interim agreement," he said.

Final status talks were due to have begun this week but were delayed because of the crisis. Those talks -- scheduled to end by 1999 -- will tackle the thorniest issues dividing Israel and the Palestinians, including borders, Jewish settlements, refugees and Jerusalem.
Israeli police chief Assaf Hefetz said on Wednesday the construction in East Jerusalem had harmed security cooperation with the PLO and raised the likelihood of guerrilla attacks.

In the West Bank village of Beit Umar, Israeli soldiers fired teargas to disperse stone-throwers during a brief incident that ended without injuries, witnesses said. Other protests in West Bank cities passed peacefully.

An army spokesman said Israeli and Palestinian troops had stopped joint patrols in the West Bank for the first time since fierce clashes sparked by Israeli moves in Jerusalem last September. Sixty-one Arabs and 15 Israelis were killed.
Palestinian officials said they were doing all they could to prevent violence but warned an angry outburst was inevitable.
"We are (headed) for an explosion," said Faisal al-Husseini, the PLO's top official in Jerusalem.
"When it will start, what will be the spark, I don't know. But I can be sure...that an explosion is coming if the situation will not be changed."
